title: Wavelet Transform
body:
A **wavelet transform** expands a signal in a basis of short, localised bumps (wavelets) instead
of the infinitely long sines and cosines of a Fourier expansion. The basis is generated from one
mother wavelet by shifting it along the signal and scaling it up and down, so each coefficient
answers **"how much of this frequency, and where"** rather than just "how much of this frequency".

That is the entire selling point. The discrete Fourier transform (named without a link here on
purpose: [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] owns it) turns a data vector into frequency amplitudes
and destroys all location information, which is fine for a steady tone and useless for a click, an
edge, or a heartbeat. Wavelets trade some frequency resolution for time resolution and keep both.

**Multi-resolution analysis** is the structure underneath: repeatedly split the signal into a
coarse approximation and the detail lost in coarsening, then recurse on the approximation. The
result is a pyramid of scales, each one an [[Orthonormal Basis]] expansion, and each level's
coefficients are [[Projection|projections]] exactly as in every other transform on this syllabus.
Most of them come out near zero for real signals, which is why JPEG 2000 and most modern
compression are wavelet based: threshold the small coefficients away and reconstruct. Same
argument as [[Low-Rank Approximation]], different basis.

## Related

- [[Orthonormal Basis]] and [[Projection]]: a transform is a change of basis, nothing more
- [[Orthogonal Functions]] and [[Fourier Series]]: the continuous, non-localised case
- [[Image Processing]]: compression and denoising in two dimensions
- [[Fourier Transform]] and [[Discrete Fourier Transform]]: the transform this one is
  the localised alternative to. The trade-off it manages is the scaling property, that narrow in
  time forces wide in frequency
